The deeper worry is that activation steering is evaluated almost entirely by its effect on the target feature and downstream behavior, while collateral suppression of co-substrate features may be subtle, nonlocal across layers, and invisible to probes that only check the steered layer — meaning you can run a clean-looking intervention study and still be systematically disrupting unrelated capabilities.

Concretely, if head H uses a Q-projection W_Q that has non-trivial inner product with the steering vector, the query changes, which alters softmax attention weights over all positions, modifying which value vectors are written back into the residual stream; this corrupts feature G's computation even though the steering vector never directly touched G's feature direction. Wang et al.'s IOI circuit work (2022) makes this precise: individual heads like the S-inhibition heads are bottlenecks through which multiple higher-level features route, so perturbing anything upstream that influences those heads' attention patterns has cascading effects on all features that read from them. A secondary mechanism is MLP neuron input redistribution: if a steered residual stream changes the pre-activation input to a shared MLP layer, neurons operating near their activation threshold can switch on or off, altering which features those neurons contribute to downstream — again fully decoupled from residual-stream direction overlap. To isolate head-mediated interference from direct crosstalk, you would apply the steering vector and then perform activation patching at the head output (patching H's output back to its unsteered value) and measure whether feature G's downstream representation recovers; if it does, the interference routes through H, not through direct residual-stream overlap. A cleaner variant freezes the attention pattern of H (using pattern-patching as in Jain et al. 2023 / Conmy et al. ACDC) while allowing the value aggregation to vary, which separates query-key competition effects from value-content effects. You would need at least two input distributions — one where feature G is active and F is not, one where both are active — and show that the patching recovery is distribution-selective, ruling out the confound that you are simply restoring global residual-stream statistics rather than feature-specific computation.

Partial recovery under head-output patching is a topological signature: it means feature G's circuit is not a simple linear chain through H but has either (a) parallel computational paths that bypass H and were also disrupted by the steering vector, or (b) upstream information loss where the inputs to H were already corrupted before H processed them, so patching H's output reinstates what H would have computed given clean inputs but not what it actually computed — and these two failure modes have opposite implications for where intervention should be targeted. The cleanest discriminant is layerwise input patching: patch the residual stream entering H (rather than exiting it) back to its unsteered value, then let H recompute naturally; if recovery improves relative to output patching, the residual non-recovery in output patching was due to upstream destruction — H's output was wrong because its input was wrong, and you were patching in a correct output that didn't match what H would have produced. Conversely, if input-to-H patching yields the same partial recovery as output-from-H patching, the missing signal was never flowing through H in the first place, implicating parallel paths — which you then localize by iteratively patching candidate parallel edges, exactly the procedure ACDC (Conmy et al., NeurIPS 2023) automates via gradient-based edge knockouts. The Indirect Object Identification circuit again provides a concrete reference: Conmy et al. found that several name-mover heads contribute independently to the final logit, so patching any single one yields partial recovery with the residual attributable to the others, a pattern that looks identical superficially to upstream destruction. A quantitative separator is path patching with attribution scores: compute the total effect of the steering perturbation on G's representation, then sum individual path effects through H versus through candidate parallel edges; if path effects through H account for less than ~50% of total effect (as measured by logit-lens or probing at G's SAE feature direction), parallel paths dominate. The remaining ambiguity — when upstream destruction and parallel paths co-occur — requires causal scrubbing (Chan et al., 2022), which tests whether a proposed circuit graph is sufficient by replacing all non-circuit activations with corrupted baselines and checking if the circuit subgraph alone reproduces the original behavior; failure here with a single-path hypothesis but success after adding parallel edges directly distinguishes the two cases without confound.

When no such window exists (P1 and P2 of G straddle F's critical layer), direction-based selectivity in the residual stream is insufficient, and you must shift strategy: either use token-position-specific steering if F and G are active at different sequence positions, or decompose the steering vector into head-input space and craft a perturbation that lies in the null space of both W_Q and W_K for the heads shared by G's paths — a much harder constraint that may have no solution if F and G share all critical heads. This is not an engineering failure but a representational entanglement theorem: if F and G require contradictory transformations from a shared layer's weights (e.g., head H must attend to position i for F and position j for G simultaneously), no additive intervention on the residual stream can satisfy both constraints, and the limit is set by the rank of the shared weight matrices relative to the number of co-active features, echoing the superposition arguments in Elhage et al. For control, it implies that fine-grained behavioral steering in a heavily superposed model is provably limited to the granularity of the circuit substrate, not the granularity of the feature space — you can steer at the resolution of shared computational modules, not individual features. Architectures that would structurally widen steering windows are those that enforce modularity through routing sparsity: Mixture-of-Experts models where different expert subnetworks handle disjoint feature sets give F and G non-overlapping computational substrates by construction, and empirical work on MoE routing (Fedus et al., Switch Transformer, 2022) shows expert specialization does emerge, though imperfectly. The constraint set scales as O(L × K² × d_router) where L is the number of MoE layers, K is the number of experts per layer, and d_router is the dimension of the router's projection space: at each MoE layer, the dangerous decision boundaries are defined by the pairwise differences of expert embedding vectors (the rows of the router weight matrix W_r), giving K(K-1)/2 boundary normals per layer, each living in the residual stream space of dimension d_model — for a model like Mixtral 8x7B with 32 MoE layers and 8 experts, this yields approximately 32 × 28 = 896 boundary normal vectors in a ~4096-dimensional space, meaning the orthogonality constraints alone consume roughly 22% of the ambient dimensions before any consideration of which boundaries are actually dangerous. The feasibility threshold is reached when the dimension of the null space of the constraint matrix — the space of vectors orthogonal to all dangerous boundary normals — drops below the intrinsic dimensionality of the target feature's causal effect, which Zou et al. The critical breakdown point can be estimated by computing the effective rank of the dangerous boundary normal matrix and comparing it to d_model minus the target feature's required projection dimension; for large MoE models with many layers and weak expert specialization, this breakdown likely occurs before all layers are constrained, meaning there is a maximum number of MoE layers beyond which router-aware steering becomes geometrically infeasible for any nontrivial target feature — a threshold no current work has computed explicitly.
